It is also said that the two words are the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "They are among the companions of the Garden." ﴿Wa'da al-sidq alladhi kanu yu'adun﴾ ("a true promise which they were promised") is a verbal noun emphasising the content of the preceding sentence, because His saying ﴿Ula'ika alladhina natagabbalu 'anhum﴾ ("Those are they from whom We accept [the best of] what they did") and what follows is in the sense of a promise of acceptance and forgiveness. It may also be a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning: God promised them a true promise, which they were promised through the tongues of the Messengers in this world.

(p-1365) Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim have narrated, and al-Hakim declared it sound, from Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) set out, and I was with him, until we entered the synagogue of the Jews on their day of festival. They disliked our entering upon them. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'O assembly of Jews, show me twelve men from among you who testify that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God; God will remove from every Jew under the canopy of heaven the wrath that is upon him.' They were silent, and none of them answered him. He repeated it to them, and none answered him, three times. He said: 'Have you refused? By God, I am the one who gathers (*al-hashir*), I am the last (*al-'aqib*), and I am the one who follows (*al-muqaffi*). Whether you believe or disbelieve.' Then he turned away, and I was with him, until we were almost leaving. Then a man came from behind him and said: 'Stay as you are, O Muhammad.' So he turned back. That man said: 'What kind of man do you know me to be among you, O assembly of Jews?' They said: 'By God, we know no man among us more knowledgeable in the Book of God, nor more learned, than you, nor than your father, nor than your grandfather.' He said: 'I testify by God that he is the Prophet whom you find written in the Torah and the Gospel.' They said: 'You have lied.' Then they turned against him and said evil things. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'You have lied. Your word will not be accepted from you.' We left, the three of us: the Messenger of God (ﷺ), myself, and Ibn Salam. Then God revealed ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from God and you disbelieve in it...﴾ until His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "I did not hear the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say to anyone walking on the face of the earth that he is among the people of the Garden, except for Abdullah ibn Salam. And concerning him was revealed ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to the like of it﴾."

al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: "Verses of the Book of God were revealed concerning me: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified﴾ was revealed concerning me, and ﴿Say: God is sufficient as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ was revealed concerning me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified﴾ that he said: "It is Abdullah ibn Salam." A similar report has been transmitted from a group of the Followers (*tabi'un*).

In this there is evidence that this verse is Medinan, so the general statement of those who say that the whole of Surat al-Ahqaf is Meccan is to be specified by it.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada, who said: "Some of the polytheists said: 'We are more honourable, and we are, and we are. Had it been good, such-and-such and such-and-such would not have preceded us to it.' So God revealed ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed: Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Awn ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab had a slave-woman who had embraced Islam before him, called Zunayra. Umar used to beat her for her Islam. The disbelieving Quraysh used to say: 'Had it been good, Zunayra would not have preceded us to it.' So God revealed concerning her ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, the verse."

al-Tabarani narrated from Samura ibn Jundub that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "32 Banu Ghifar and Aslam were a trial for many people, who say: 'Had it been good, God would not have made them the first of the people to it.'"

Ibn Asakir narrated through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The statement of Him: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents﴾, the verse, down to His saying: ﴿a true promise which they were promised﴾, was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Nafi' ibn Jubayr that Ibn Abbas informed him, saying: "I am the companion of the woman who was brought to Umar, having given birth after six months. People denied it. I said to Umar: 'Why are you wronging her?' He said: 'How?' I said: 'Recite ﴿And its carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾ and ﴿The mothers suckle their children two complete years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]. How many is the year?' He said: 'A year.' I said: 'How many is the year?' He said: 'Twelve months.' I said: 'Then twenty-four months are two complete years, and God delays from the pregnancy what He wills and hastens what He wills.' So Umar was content with my statement."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he used to say: "If a woman gives birth at nine months, twenty-one months of suckling suffice her. If she gives birth at seven months, twenty-three months of suckling suffice her. If she gives birth at six months, then two complete years, because God says: ﴿And its carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him: "This verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq: ﴿until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years, he says: My Lord, enable me﴾, the verse. God answered him, so his parents both embraced Islam, and all his brothers and his children. And concerning him was also revealed ﴿As for he who gives and fears God﴾ [al-Layl: 5], down to the end of the surah."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 46, verse 10–16 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Say: Tell me﴾, i.e., inform me, ﴿if it is from Allah﴾, meaning what is revealed to him of the Qur'an. It was also said that the intended one is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the meaning is: if he was sent from other than Allah. His saying, "and you have disbelieved in it," is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with qad implied. Likewise His saying, ﴿and a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾. The meaning is: inform me if that is in reality from Allah while you have disbelieved in it, and a witness from the Children of Israel, the knowledgeable ones in what Allah sent down in the Torah, testified to its like, i.e., to the Qur'an, from the meanings present in the Torah that agree with it, such as the affirmation of tawhid, resurrection, rising from the graves, and other things.

This likeness is in terms of the agreement of meanings, even though the wordings differ.

Al-Jurjani said: "mithl" is a connecting particle (ṣilah), and the meaning is: a witness testified concerning it that it is from Allah. Al-Wahidi said the same.

So the witness believed in the Qur'an when it became clear to him that it is the speech of Allah and of the same kind as what He sends down to His messengers. This witness from the Children of Israel is ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, as said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, ʿIkrimah, and others. But this is open to question, for the surah is Meccan by consensus, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam embraced Islam after the Hijrah. So the witness must be a man from the People of the Book who believed in the Qur'an in Mecca and affirmed it. Ibn Jarir chose this view. Later in the discussion there will be what shows that it is ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and that this verse is Medinan, not Meccan.

It is narrated from Masruq that the man intended is Musa (peace be upon him). His saying, "and you were arrogant," is conjoined to "testified": i.e., the witness believed, and you were arrogant about belief. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾: Allah, glory be to Him, deprives them of guidance because of their wronging themselves by disbelief after the clear proof of the obligation of belief has been established. Whoever loses Allah's guidance goes astray.

There has been disagreement about what the answer to the condition is. Al-Zajjaj said it is omitted, its implied meaning being: "Will you then believe?" It was also said that the answer is His saying, ﴿then you believed and were arrogant﴾. It was also said that it is omitted, its implied meaning being: "then you have wronged," as indicated by ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. It was also said that its implied meaning is: "then who is more astray than you," as in His saying: ﴿Tell me, if it is from Allah and you have disbelieved in it, who is more astray?﴾ [Fussilat: 52], and so on.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said its implied meaning is: "Do you feel secure from the punishment of Allah?" It was also said the implied meaning is: "Are you not wrongdoers?"

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another type of their false statements, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said of those who believed﴾, i.e., concerning them. It is possible that this lām is the lām of communication (lām al-tablīgh). ﴿"Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it."﴾ i.e., had what Muhammad brought of the Qur'an and prophethood been good, they would not have preceded us to it, for in their own view they deserved to precede others to every honour. They did not know that Allah, glory be to Him, singles out with His mercy whomever He wills, honours whomever He wills, humbles whomever He wills, and chooses for His religion whomever He wills. ﴿And since they have not been guided by it﴾: i.e., by the Qur'an. It was said: by Muhammad (ﷺ), and it was said: by belief. ﴿They will say, "This is an ancient falsehood."﴾ They went beyond denying the goodness of the Qur'an to claiming that it is an ancient lie, as they said: "Tales of the ancients." The agent of "idh" is an implied verb: i.e., their obstinacy became manifest. The verb "fasayaqulun" cannot govern it, because of the contradiction between the two times, namely the past and the future, and also because of the fa'. It was said that its agent is an implied verb of the same kind as what is mentioned: i.e., "they were not guided by it." And when they were not guided by it, then "they will say."

﴿And before it was the Book of Musa﴾. The majority read the mim of "min" with a kasra, as a preposition, and with its genitive it is a predicate preceding; "the Book of Musa" is a postponed subject. The clause is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial clause, or it is a new independent clause, and the discourse is directed to refute their saying "an ancient falsehood," for the fact that the Book of Musa preceded the Qur'an, and that the two agreed in the foundations of the sharia, shows that it is true and from Allah, and this requires the invalidity of their saying.

It was also read with a fatha on the mim of "man," as a relative pronoun, and with "kitab" in the accusative: i.e., "and We gave to those before him the Book of Musa." This reading is reported from al-Kalbi.

﴿As an imam and a mercy﴾: i.e., one who is followed in religion, and a mercy from Allah for those who believe in it. Both are accusative as circumstantial clauses, as said by al-Zajjaj and others. Al-Akhfash said they are accusative as absolute/detached, and Abu ʿUbayda said: i.e., We made it an imam and a mercy. ﴿And this is a Book confirming﴾: meaning the Qur'an, for it confirms the Book of Musa, which is an imam and a mercy, and other books of Allah. It was also said: it confirms the Prophet (ﷺ). The accusative of ﴿in Arabic tongue﴾ is a preparatory circumstantial clause, its referent being the pronoun in "confirming," which refers to "Book." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be an object of "confirming," but the first is better. It was also said that it is by omission of an annexed noun: i.e., possessor of an Arabic tongue, and this is the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿To warn those who have done wrong﴾. The majority read "liyundhira" with the yā' (third person), its subject being a pronoun referring to the Book: i.e., that the Book warn those who have done wrong. It was also said the pronoun refers to Allah, and it was said to the Messenger, and the first is better.

Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, and al-Bazzi read it with the tā' (second person), its subject being the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Hatim and Abu ʿUbayd chose this reading. His saying, ﴿and good tidings to the good-doers﴾, is in the place of an accusative, conjoined to the place of "liyundhira." Al-Zajjaj said the better view is that it is in the place of a nominative: i.e., and it is good tidings. It was also said it is in the verbal-noun sense (maṣdar) by an implied verb: i.e., and [it] gives good tidings. His saying "lil-muhsinin" is connected to "bushra."

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast﴾: i.e., they combined tawhid with steadfastness upon the sharia. The explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-Sajdah. ﴿There will be no fear for them﴾: the fa' is extra in the predicate of the relative clause because it has the meaning of a condition. ﴿Nor will they grieve﴾. The meaning: they do not fear that any harm will befall them, nor do they grieve over the loss of something beloved, and that this is continuous and permanent.

﴿Those are the companions of Paradise﴾: i.e., those described with what was mentioned are the companions of Paradise, the abode of believers, while abiding therein forever. In this verse there is a great matter of encouragement, for the negation of fear and grief permanently and stably in Paradise forever is something souls seek above all else and do not long for anything other than it. ﴿As a reward for what they used to do﴾: i.e., they are recompensed because of their deeds, which they performed by way of acts of obedience to Allah and abstention from His disobediences.

﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾. The majority read "ḥusnan" with a ḍammah on the ḥā' and sukūn on the sīn. ʿAli and al-Sulami read both with a fatḥah. Ibn ʿAbbas and the Kufans read "iḥsānan," which has already been discussed in Surah al-ʿAnkabut: "And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents," without disagreement among the readers, and it has been discussed in Surah al-Anʿam and Surah Banu Isra'il: "and to parents, kindness" (al-Isra': 23). Perhaps this is the reason for the readers' difference in this verse. In all these readings its accusative is a verbal-noun form: i.e., We enjoined him to be kind to both of them, with kindness. It was also said it is an object by the verb "waṣṣaynā" being given the sense of "alzamnā" (obliged). It was also said it is an object of purpose.

﴿His mother bore him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship﴾. The majority read "kurhan" in both places with a ḍammah on the kāf. Abu ʿAmr and the people of the Hijaz read both with a fatḥah. Al-Kisa'i said: they are two dialects with one meaning. Abu Hatim said: "al-karh" with a fatḥah is not fitting, because it means anger and overpowering. Abu ʿUbayd chose the reading with a fatḥah, saying: because the word "al-karh" throughout the Qur'an is with a fatḥah, except in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you while it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. It was also said that "kurh" with a ḍammah is what a person imposes on himself, and with a fatḥah is what is imposed on him by others.

Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the mother's bearing and birth only to emphasize the obligation of kindness to her, which Allah has enjoined. The meaning: she carried him in a state of hardship and gave birth to him in a state of hardship.

Then He, glory be to Him, specified the period of his carrying and weaning, saying: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾: i.e., the duration of both is this period, from the beginning of his carrying until he is weaned from breastfeeding, i.e., is turned away from it. This verse has been used as evidence that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months, because the full period of breastfeeding is two years, as in His saying: ﴿two full years for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]. So He, glory be to Him, mentioned in this verse the minimum period of pregnancy and the maximum period of breastfeeding.

In this verse there is an indication that the mother's right is more emphatic than the father's right, for she carried him with difficulty, gave birth to him with difficulty, and nursed him for this period with fatigue and toil, and the father did not share with her in any of that.

The majority read "wa-fiṣāluhu" with an alif. Al-Hasan, Yaʿqub, Qatadah, and al-Jahdari read "wa-faṣluhu" with a fatḥah on the fā' and sukūn on the ṣād, without an alif. "Al-faṣl" and "al-fiṣāl" have the same meaning, like "al-fiṭm" and "al-fiṭām," and "al-qaṭf" and "al-qiṭāf."

﴿Until, when he reaches his full strength﴾: i.e., he reaches the maturity of his strength and intellect. The reality of "ashudd" has already been discussed fully. It is necessary to posit a clause for which "ḥattā" is the limit: i.e., he lived and his life continued until he reached his full strength. It was said he reached the age of eighteen years. It was also said: "ashudd" is puberty, as said by al-Sha'bi and Ibn Zayd. Al-Hasan said it is reaching forty years, but the first is better because of His saying: ﴿and reaches forty years﴾, for this indicates that reaching forty is something beyond reaching "ashudd."

The exegetes said: Allah never sent a prophet except after forty years.

﴿He says, "My Lord, inspire me"﴾: i.e., inspire me. Al-Jawhari said: "istawza'tu Allah fa-awza'anī," i.e., I asked Allah for inspiration and He inspired me. ﴿to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents﴾: i.e., inspire me to thank You for what You have bestowed upon me of guidance, and upon my parents for their tenderness toward me when they raised me as a child. It was also said: You have bestowed upon me health and well-being, and upon my parents wealth and affluence. The better view is not to restrict the favour upon him, or upon his parents, to a specific favour. ﴿And that I do righteous deeds which You approve﴾: i.e., inspire me to do a righteous deed that You approve from me. ﴿And make righteous for me my offspring﴾: i.e., make my descendants righteous, firmly established in righteousness and capable of it.

This verse is evidence that whoever reaches the age of forty should abundantly make these supplications. It has been reported that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, as will come later in the discussion. ﴿Indeed, I have repented to You﴾ from my sins, ﴿and indeed I am of the Muslims﴾: i.e., those who submit to You, who comply with Your obedience, and who are sincere in Your tawhid.

The reference in "those" is to the human mentioned, and the plural is used because the intended meaning is the genus. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿those from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾ of good deeds in this world. "The best" here means "the good," as in His saying: ﴿and follow the best of what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Zumar: 55]. It was also said that the comparative is on its real meaning, and what is intended is what the servant is rewarded for among deeds, not what he is not rewarded for, such as the permissible, which is good but not the best. ﴿And We overlook their misdeeds﴾, so We do not punish them for them.

The majority read "yutaqabbalu" and "yatajāwazu" with both verbs in the passive form.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verb with the *nun* (*nakhāwazu*, "We pass over") in both places, attributing it to God, glorified is He. *Al-tajawuz* means forgiveness. Its root is from *juztu al-shay'*, meaning "I passed beyond the thing" when you did not stop at it. The phrase ﴿fi ashab al-jannah﴾ ("among the companions of the Garden") means that they are among their number and included in their ranks. The prepositional phrase is in the accusative position as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, a clause describing the state of the subject) on the model of your saying: "The commander honoured me *fi ashabihi* (among his companions)," meaning: being within their body. It is said that *fi* here carries the sense of *ma'a* (with), meaning: "with the companions of the Garden." It is also said that the two words are the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "They are among the companions of the Garden." ﴿Wa'da al-sidq alladhi kanu yu'adun﴾ ("a true promise which they were promised") is a verbal noun emphasising the content of the preceding sentence, because His saying ﴿Ula'ika alladhina natagabbalu 'anhum﴾ ("Those are they from whom We accept [the best of] what they did") and what follows is in the sense of a promise of acceptance and forgiveness. It may also be a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning: God promised them a true promise, which they were promised through the tongues of the Messengers in this world.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 46, verse 10–16 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Say: Tell me﴾, i.e., inform me, ﴿if it is from Allah﴾, meaning what is revealed to him of the Qur'an. It was also said that the intended one is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the meaning is: if he was sent from other than Allah. His saying, "and you have disbelieved in it," is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with qad implied. Likewise His saying, ﴿and a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾. The meaning is: inform me if that is in reality from Allah while you have disbelieved in it, and a witness from the Children of Israel, the knowledgeable ones in what Allah sent down in the Torah, testified to its like, i.e., to the Qur'an, from the meanings present in the Torah that agree with it, such as the affirmation of tawhid, resurrection, rising from the graves, and other things.

This likeness is in terms of the agreement of meanings, even though the wordings differ.

Al-Jurjani said: "mithl" is a connecting particle (ṣilah), and the meaning is: a witness testified concerning it that it is from Allah. Al-Wahidi said the same.

So the witness believed in the Qur'an when it became clear to him that it is the speech of Allah and of the same kind as what He sends down to His messengers. This witness from the Children of Israel is ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, as said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, ʿIkrimah, and others. But this is open to question, for the surah is Meccan by consensus, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam embraced Islam after the Hijrah. So the witness must be a man from the People of the Book who believed in the Qur'an in Mecca and affirmed it. Ibn Jarir chose this view. Later in the discussion there will be what shows that it is ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and that this verse is Medinan, not Meccan.

It is narrated from Masruq that the man intended is Musa (peace be upon him). His saying, "and you were arrogant," is conjoined to "testified": i.e., the witness believed, and you were arrogant about belief. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾: Allah, glory be to Him, deprives them of guidance because of their wronging themselves by disbelief after the clear proof of the obligation of belief has been established. Whoever loses Allah's guidance goes astray.

There has been disagreement about what the answer to the condition is. Al-Zajjaj said it is omitted, its implied meaning being: "Will you then believe?" It was also said that the answer is His saying, ﴿then you believed and were arrogant﴾. It was also said that it is omitted, its implied meaning being: "then you have wronged," as indicated by ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. It was also said that its implied meaning is: "then who is more astray than you," as in His saying: ﴿Tell me, if it is from Allah and you have disbelieved in it, who is more astray?﴾ [Fussilat: 52], and so on.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said its implied meaning is: "Do you feel secure from the punishment of Allah?" It was also said the implied meaning is: "Are you not wrongdoers?"

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another type of their false statements, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said of those who believed﴾, i.e., concerning them. It is possible that this lām is the lām of communication (lām al-tablīgh). ﴿"Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it."﴾ i.e., had what Muhammad brought of the Qur'an and prophethood been good, they would not have preceded us to it, for in their own view they deserved to precede others to every honour. They did not know that Allah, glory be to Him, singles out with His mercy whomever He wills, honours whomever He wills, humbles whomever He wills, and chooses for His religion whomever He wills. ﴿And since they have not been guided by it﴾: i.e., by the Qur'an. It was said: by Muhammad (ﷺ), and it was said: by belief. ﴿They will say, "This is an ancient falsehood."﴾ They went beyond denying the goodness of the Qur'an to claiming that it is an ancient lie, as they said: "Tales of the ancients." The agent of "idh" is an implied verb: i.e., their obstinacy became manifest. The verb "fasayaqulun" cannot govern it, because of the contradiction between the two times, namely the past and the future, and also because of the fa'. It was said that its agent is an implied verb of the same kind as what is mentioned: i.e., "they were not guided by it." And when they were not guided by it, then "they will say."

﴿And before it was the Book of Musa﴾. The majority read the mim of "min" with a kasra, as a preposition, and with its genitive it is a predicate preceding; "the Book of Musa" is a postponed subject. The clause is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial clause, or it is a new independent clause, and the discourse is directed to refute their saying "an ancient falsehood," for the fact that the Book of Musa preceded the Qur'an, and that the two agreed in the foundations of the sharia, shows that it is true and from Allah, and this requires the invalidity of their saying.

It was also read with a fatha on the mim of "man," as a relative pronoun, and with "kitab" in the accusative: i.e., "and We gave to those before him the Book of Musa." This reading is reported from al-Kalbi.

﴿As an imam and a mercy﴾: i.e., one who is followed in religion, and a mercy from Allah for those who believe in it. Both are accusative as circumstantial clauses, as said by al-Zajjaj and others. Al-Akhfash said they are accusative as absolute/detached, and Abu ʿUbayda said: i.e., We made it an imam and a mercy. ﴿And this is a Book confirming﴾: meaning the Qur'an, for it confirms the Book of Musa, which is an imam and a mercy, and other books of Allah. It was also said: it confirms the Prophet (ﷺ). The accusative of ﴿in Arabic tongue﴾ is a preparatory circumstantial clause, its referent being the pronoun in "confirming," which refers to "Book." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be an object of "confirming," but the first is better. It was also said that it is by omission of an annexed noun: i.e., possessor of an Arabic tongue, and this is the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿To warn those who have done wrong﴾. The majority read "liyundhira" with the yā' (third person), its subject being a pronoun referring to the Book: i.e., that the Book warn those who have done wrong. It was also said the pronoun refers to Allah, and it was said to the Messenger, and the first is better.

Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, and al-Bazzi read it with the tā' (second person), its subject being the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Hatim and Abu ʿUbayd chose this reading. His saying, ﴿and good tidings to the good-doers﴾, is in the place of an accusative, conjoined to the place of "liyundhira." Al-Zajjaj said the better view is that it is in the place of a nominative: i.e., and it is good tidings. It was also said it is in the verbal-noun sense (maṣdar) by an implied verb: i.e., and [it] gives good tidings. His saying "lil-muhsinin" is connected to "bushra."

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast﴾: i.e., they combined tawhid with steadfastness upon the sharia. The explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-Sajdah. ﴿There will be no fear for them﴾: the fa' is extra in the predicate of the relative clause because it has the meaning of a condition. ﴿Nor will they grieve﴾. The meaning: they do not fear that any harm will befall them, nor do they grieve over the loss of something beloved, and that this is continuous and permanent.

﴿Those are the companions of Paradise﴾: i.e., those described with what was mentioned are the companions of Paradise, the abode of believers, while abiding therein forever. In this verse there is a great matter of encouragement, for the negation of fear and grief permanently and stably in Paradise forever is something souls seek above all else and do not long for anything other than it. ﴿As a reward for what they used to do﴾: i.e., they are recompensed because of their deeds, which they performed by way of acts of obedience to Allah and abstention from His disobediences.

﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾. The majority read "ḥusnan" with a ḍammah on the ḥā' and sukūn on the sīn. ʿAli and al-Sulami read both with a fatḥah. Ibn ʿAbbas and the Kufans read "iḥsānan," which has already been discussed in Surah al-ʿAnkabut: "And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents," without disagreement among the readers, and it has been discussed in Surah al-Anʿam and Surah Banu Isra'il: "and to parents, kindness" (al-Isra': 23). Perhaps this is the reason for the readers' difference in this verse. In all these readings its accusative is a verbal-noun form: i.e., We enjoined him to be kind to both of them, with kindness. It was also said it is an object by the verb "waṣṣaynā" being given the sense of "alzamnā" (obliged). It was also said it is an object of purpose.

﴿His mother bore him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship﴾. The majority read "kurhan" in both places with a ḍammah on the kāf. Abu ʿAmr and the people of the Hijaz read both with a fatḥah. Al-Kisa'i said: they are two dialects with one meaning. Abu Hatim said: "al-karh" with a fatḥah is not fitting, because it means anger and overpowering. Abu ʿUbayd chose the reading with a fatḥah, saying: because the word "al-karh" throughout the Qur'an is with a fatḥah, except in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you while it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. It was also said that "kurh" with a ḍammah is what a person imposes on himself, and with a fatḥah is what is imposed on him by others.

Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the mother's bearing and birth only to emphasize the obligation of kindness to her, which Allah has enjoined. The meaning: she carried him in a state of hardship and gave birth to him in a state of hardship.

Then He, glory be to Him, specified the period of his carrying and weaning, saying: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾: i.e., the duration of both is this period, from the beginning of his carrying until he is weaned from breastfeeding, i.e., is turned away from it. This verse has been used as evidence that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months, because the full period of breastfeeding is two years, as in His saying: ﴿two full years for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]. So He, glory be to Him, mentioned in this verse the minimum period of pregnancy and the maximum period of breastfeeding.

In this verse there is an indication that the mother's right is more emphatic than the father's right, for she carried him with difficulty, gave birth to him with difficulty, and nursed him for this period with fatigue and toil, and the father did not share with her in any of that.

The majority read "wa-fiṣāluhu" with an alif. Al-Hasan, Yaʿqub, Qatadah, and al-Jahdari read "wa-faṣluhu" with a fatḥah on the fā' and sukūn on the ṣād, without an alif. "Al-faṣl" and "al-fiṣāl" have the same meaning, like "al-fiṭm" and "al-fiṭām," and "al-qaṭf" and "al-qiṭāf."

﴿Until, when he reaches his full strength﴾: i.e., he reaches the maturity of his strength and intellect. The reality of "ashudd" has already been discussed fully. It is necessary to posit a clause for which "ḥattā" is the limit: i.e., he lived and his life continued until he reached his full strength. It was said he reached the age of eighteen years. It was also said: "ashudd" is puberty, as said by al-Sha'bi and Ibn Zayd. Al-Hasan said it is reaching forty years, but the first is better because of His saying: ﴿and reaches forty years﴾, for this indicates that reaching forty is something beyond reaching "ashudd."

The exegetes said: Allah never sent a prophet except after forty years.

﴿He says, "My Lord, inspire me"﴾: i.e., inspire me. Al-Jawhari said: "istawza'tu Allah fa-awza'anī," i.e., I asked Allah for inspiration and He inspired me. ﴿to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents﴾: i.e., inspire me to thank You for what You have bestowed upon me of guidance, and upon my parents for their tenderness toward me when they raised me as a child. It was also said: You have bestowed upon me health and well-being, and upon my parents wealth and affluence. The better view is not to restrict the favour upon him, or upon his parents, to a specific favour. ﴿And that I do righteous deeds which You approve﴾: i.e., inspire me to do a righteous deed that You approve from me. ﴿And make righteous for me my offspring﴾: i.e., make my descendants righteous, firmly established in righteousness and capable of it.

This verse is evidence that whoever reaches the age of forty should abundantly make these supplications. It has been reported that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, as will come later in the discussion. ﴿Indeed, I have repented to You﴾ from my sins, ﴿and indeed I am of the Muslims﴾: i.e., those who submit to You, who comply with Your obedience, and who are sincere in Your tawhid.

The reference in "those" is to the human mentioned, and the plural is used because the intended meaning is the genus. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿those from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾ of good deeds in this world. "The best" here means "the good," as in His saying: ﴿and follow the best of what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Zumar: 55]. It was also said that the comparative is on its real meaning, and what is intended is what the servant is rewarded for among deeds, not what he is not rewarded for, such as the permissible, which is good but not the best. ﴿And We overlook their misdeeds﴾, so We do not punish them for them.

The majority read "yutaqabbalu" and "yatajāwazu" with both verbs in the passive form.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verb with the *nun* (*nakhāwazu*, "We pass over") in both places, attributing it to God, glorified is He. *Al-tajawuz* means forgiveness. Its root is from *juztu al-shay'*, meaning "I passed beyond the thing" when you did not stop at it. The phrase ﴿fi ashab al-jannah﴾ ("among the companions of the Garden") means that they are among their number and included in their ranks. The prepositional phrase is in the accusative position as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, a clause describing the state of the subject) on the model of your saying: "The commander honoured me *fi ashabihi* (among his companions)," meaning: being within their body. It is said that *fi* here carries the sense of *ma'a* (with), meaning: "with the companions of the Garden." It is also said that the two words are the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "They are among the companions of the Garden." ﴿Wa'da al-sidq alladhi kanu yu'adun﴾ ("a true promise which they were promised") is a verbal noun emphasising the content of the preceding sentence, because His saying ﴿Ula'ika alladhina natagabbalu 'anhum﴾ ("Those are they from whom We accept [the best of] what they did") and what follows is in the sense of a promise of acceptance and forgiveness. It may also be a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning: God promised them a true promise, which they were promised through the tongues of the Messengers in this world.

(p-1365) Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim have narrated, and al-Hakim declared it sound, from Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) set out, and I was with him, until we entered the synagogue of the Jews on their day of festival. They disliked our entering upon them. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'O assembly of Jews, show me twelve men from among you who testify that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God; God will remove from every Jew under the canopy of heaven the wrath that is upon him.' They were silent, and none of them answered him. He repeated it to them, and none answered him, three times. He said: 'Have you refused? By God, I am the one who gathers (*al-hashir*), I am the last (*al-'aqib*), and I am the one who follows (*al-muqaffi*). Whether you believe or disbelieve.' Then he turned away, and I was with him, until we were almost leaving. Then a man came from behind him and said: 'Stay as you are, O Muhammad.' So he turned back. That man said: 'What kind of man do you know me to be among you, O assembly of Jews?' They said: 'By God, we know no man among us more knowledgeable in the Book of God, nor more learned, than you, nor than your father, nor than your grandfather.' He said: 'I testify by God that he is the Prophet whom you find written in the Torah and the Gospel.' They said: 'You have lied.' Then they turned against him and said evil things. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'You have lied. Your word will not be accepted from you.' We left, the three of us: the Messenger of God (ﷺ), myself, and Ibn Salam. Then God revealed ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from God and you disbelieve in it...﴾ until His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "I did not hear the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say to anyone walking on the face of the earth that he is among the people of the Garden, except for Abdullah ibn Salam. And concerning him was revealed ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to the like of it﴾."

al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: "Verses of the Book of God were revealed concerning me: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified﴾ was revealed concerning me, and ﴿Say: God is sufficient as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ was revealed concerning me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified﴾ that he said: "It is Abdullah ibn Salam." A similar report has been transmitted from a group of the Followers (*tabi'un*).

In this there is evidence that this verse is Medinan, so the general statement of those who say that the whole of Surat al-Ahqaf is Meccan is to be specified by it.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada, who said: "Some of the polytheists said: 'We are more honourable, and we are, and we are. Had it been good, such-and-such and such-and-such would not have preceded us to it.' So God revealed ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed: Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Awn ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab had a slave-woman who had embraced Islam before him, called Zunayra. Umar used to beat her for her Islam. The disbelieving Quraysh used to say: 'Had it been good, Zunayra would not have preceded us to it.' So God revealed concerning her ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, the verse."

al-Tabarani narrated from Samura ibn Jundub that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "32 Banu Ghifar and Aslam were a trial for many people, who say: 'Had it been good, God would not have made them the first of the people to it.'"

Ibn Asakir narrated through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The statement of Him: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents﴾, the verse, down to His saying: ﴿a true promise which they were promised﴾, was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Nafi' ibn Jubayr that Ibn Abbas informed him, saying: "I am the companion of the woman who was brought to Umar, having given birth after six months. People denied it. I said to Umar: 'Why are you wronging her?' He said: 'How?' I said: 'Recite ﴿And its carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾ and ﴿The mothers suckle their children two complete years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]. How many is the year?' He said: 'A year.' I said: 'How many is the year?' He said: 'Twelve months.' I said: 'Then twenty-four months are two complete years, and God delays from the pregnancy what He wills and hastens what He wills.' So Umar was content with my statement."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he used to say: "If a woman gives birth at nine months, twenty-one months of suckling suffice her. If she gives birth at seven months, twenty-three months of suckling suffice her. If she gives birth at six months, then two complete years, because God says: ﴿And its carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him: "This verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq: ﴿until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years, he says: My Lord, enable me﴾, the verse. God answered him, so his parents both embraced Islam, and all his brothers and his children. And concerning him was also revealed ﴿As for he who gives and fears God﴾ [al-Layl: 5], down to the end of the surah."

The meaning: they do not fear that any harm will befall them, nor do they grieve over the loss of something beloved, and that this is continuous and permanent.

In this verse there is a great matter of encouragement, for the negation of fear and grief permanently and stably in Paradise forever is something souls seek above all else and do not long for anything other than it. ﴿As a reward for what they used to do﴾: i.e., they are recompensed because of their deeds, which they performed by way of acts of obedience to Allah and abstention from His disobediences.

﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾. The majority read "ḥusnan" with a ḍammah on the ḥā' and sukūn on the sīn. ʿAli and al-Sulami read both with a fatḥah. Ibn ʿAbbas and the Kufans read "iḥsānan," which has already been discussed in Surah al-ʿAnkabut: "And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents," without disagreement among the readers, and it has been discussed in Surah al-Anʿam and Surah Banu Isra'il: "and to parents, kindness" (al-Isra': 23). Perhaps this is the reason for the readers' difference in this verse. In all these readings its accusative is a verbal-noun form: i.e., We enjoined him to be kind to both of them, with kindness. It was also said it is an object by the verb "waṣṣaynā" being given the sense of "alzamnā" (obliged). It was also said it is an object of purpose.

﴿His mother bore him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship﴾. The majority read "kurhan" in both places with a ḍammah on the kāf. Abu ʿAmr and the people of the Hijaz read both with a fatḥah. Al-Kisa'i said: they are two dialects with one meaning. Abu Hatim said: "al-karh" with a fatḥah is not fitting, because it means anger and overpowering. Abu ʿUbayd chose the reading with a fatḥah, saying: because the word "al-karh" throughout the Qur'an is with a fatḥah, except in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you while it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. It was also said that "kurh" with a ḍammah is what a person imposes on himself, and with a fatḥah is what is imposed on him by others.

Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the mother's bearing and birth only to emphasize the obligation of kindness to her, which Allah has enjoined. The meaning: she carried him in a state of hardship and gave birth to him in a state of hardship.

Then He, glory be to Him, specified the period of his carrying and weaning, saying: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾: i.e., the duration of both is this period, from the beginning of his carrying until he is weaned from breastfeeding, i.e., is turned away from it. This verse has been used as evidence that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months, because the full period of breastfeeding is two years, as in His saying: ﴿two full years for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]. So He, glory be to Him, mentioned in this verse the minimum period of pregnancy and the maximum period of breastfeeding.

In this verse there is an indication that the mother's right is more emphatic than the father's right, for she carried him with difficulty, gave birth to him with difficulty, and nursed him for this period with fatigue and toil, and the father did not share with her in any of that.

The majority read "wa-fiṣāluhu" with an alif. Al-Hasan, Yaʿqub, Qatadah, and al-Jahdari read "wa-faṣluhu" with a fatḥah on the fā' and sukūn on the ṣād, without an alif. "Al-faṣl" and "al-fiṣāl" have the same meaning, like "al-fiṭm" and "al-fiṭām," and "al-qaṭf" and "al-qiṭāf."

﴿Until, when he reaches his full strength﴾: i.e., he reaches the maturity of his strength and intellect. The reality of "ashudd" has already been discussed fully. It is necessary to posit a clause for which "ḥattā" is the limit: i.e., he lived and his life continued until he reached his full strength. It was said he reached the age of eighteen years. It was also said: "ashudd" is puberty, as said by al-Sha'bi and Ibn Zayd. Al-Hasan said it is reaching forty years, but the first is better because of His saying: ﴿and reaches forty years﴾, for this indicates that reaching forty is something beyond reaching "ashudd."

The exegetes said: Allah never sent a prophet except after forty years.

﴿He says, "My Lord, inspire me"﴾: i.e., inspire me. Al-Jawhari said: "istawza'tu Allah fa-awza'anī," i.e., I asked Allah for inspiration and He inspired me. ﴿to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents﴾: i.e., inspire me to thank You for what You have bestowed upon me of guidance, and upon my parents for their tenderness toward me when they raised me as a child. It was also said: You have bestowed upon me health and well-being, and upon my parents wealth and affluence. The better view is not to restrict the favour upon him, or upon his parents, to a specific favour. ﴿And that I do righteous deeds which You approve﴾: i.e., inspire me to do a righteous deed that You approve from me. ﴿And make righteous for me my offspring﴾: i.e., make my descendants righteous, firmly established in righteousness and capable of it.

This verse is evidence that whoever reaches the age of forty should abundantly make these supplications. It has been reported that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, as will come later in the discussion. ﴿Indeed, I have repented to You﴾ from my sins, ﴿and indeed I am of the Muslims﴾: i.e., those who submit to You, who comply with Your obedience, and who are sincere in Your tawhid.

The reference in "those" is to the human mentioned, and the plural is used because the intended meaning is the genus. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿those from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾ of good deeds in this world. "The best" here means "the good," as in His saying: ﴿and follow the best of what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Zumar: 55]. It was also said that the comparative is on its real meaning, and what is intended is what the servant is rewarded for among deeds, not what he is not rewarded for, such as the permissible, which is good but not the best. ﴿And We overlook their misdeeds﴾, so We do not punish them for them.

The majority read "yutaqabbalu" and "yatajāwazu" with both verbs in the passive form.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verb with the *nun* (*nakhāwazu*, "We pass over") in both places, attributing it to God, glorified is He. *Al-tajawuz* means forgiveness. Its root is from *juztu al-shay'*, meaning "I passed beyond the thing" when you did not stop at it. The phrase ﴿fi ashab al-jannah﴾ ("among the companions of the Garden") means that they are among their number and included in their ranks. The prepositional phrase is in the accusative position as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, a clause describing the state of the subject) on the model of your saying: "The commander honoured me *fi ashabihi* (among his companions)," meaning: being within their body. It is said that *fi* here carries the sense of *ma'a* (with), meaning: "with the companions of the Garden." It is also said that the two words are the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "They are among the companions of the Garden." ﴿Wa'da al-sidq alladhi kanu yu'adun﴾ ("a true promise which they were promised") is a verbal noun emphasising the content of the preceding sentence, because His saying ﴿Ula'ika alladhina natagabbalu 'anhum﴾ ("Those are they from whom We accept [the best of] what they did") and what follows is in the sense of a promise of acceptance and forgiveness. It may also be a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning: God promised them a true promise, which they were promised through the tongues of the Messengers in this world.

(p-1365) Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim have narrated, and al-Hakim declared it sound, from Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) set out, and I was with him, until we entered the synagogue of the Jews on their day of festival. They disliked our entering upon them. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'O assembly of Jews, show me twelve men from among you who testify that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God; God will remove from every Jew under the canopy of heaven the wrath that is upon him.' They were silent, and none of them answered him. He repeated it to them, and none answered him, three times. He said: 'Have you refused? By God, I am the one who gathers (*al-hashir*), I am the last (*al-'aqib*), and I am the one who follows (*al-muqaffi*). Whether you believe or disbelieve.' Then he turned away, and I was with him, until we were almost leaving. Then a man came from behind him and said: 'Stay as you are, O Muhammad.' So he turned back. That man said: 'What kind of man do you know me to be among you, O assembly of Jews?' They said: 'By God, we know no man among us more knowledgeable in the Book of God, nor more learned, than you, nor than your father, nor than your grandfather.' He said: 'I testify by God that he is the Prophet whom you find written in the Torah and the Gospel.' They said: 'You have lied.' Then they turned against him and said evil things. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'You have lied. Your word will not be accepted from you.' We left, the three of us: the Messenger of God (ﷺ), myself, and Ibn Salam. Then God revealed ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from God and you disbelieve in it...﴾ until His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "I did not hear the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say to anyone walking on the face of the earth that he is among the people of the Garden, except for Abdullah ibn Salam. And concerning him was revealed ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to the like of it﴾."

al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: "Verses of the Book of God were revealed concerning me: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified﴾ was revealed concerning me, and ﴿Say: God is sufficient as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ was revealed concerning me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified﴾ that he said: "It is Abdullah ibn Salam." A similar report has been transmitted from a group of the Followers (*tabi'un*).

In this there is evidence that this verse is Medinan, so the general statement of those who say that the whole of Surat al-Ahqaf is Meccan is to be specified by it.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada, who said: "Some of the polytheists said: 'We are more honourable, and we are, and we are. Had it been good, such-and-such and such-and-such would not have preceded us to it.' So God revealed ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed: Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Awn ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab had a slave-woman who had embraced Islam before him, called Zunayra. Umar used to beat her for her Islam. The disbelieving Quraysh used to say: 'Had it been good, Zunayra would not have preceded us to it.' So God revealed concerning her ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, the verse."

al-Tabarani narrated from Samura ibn Jundub that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "32 Banu Ghifar and Aslam were a trial for many people, who say: 'Had it been good, God would not have made them the first of the people to it.'"

Ibn Asakir narrated through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The statement of Him: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents﴾, the verse, down to His saying: ﴿a true promise which they were promised﴾, was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Nafi' ibn Jubayr that Ibn Abbas informed him, saying: "I am the companion of the woman who was brought to Umar, having given birth after six months. People denied it. I said to Umar: 'Why are you wronging her?' He said: 'How?' I said: 'Recite ﴿And its carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾ and ﴿The mothers suckle their children two complete years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]. How many is the year?' He said: 'A year.' I said: 'How many is the year?' He said: 'Twelve months.' I said: 'Then twenty-four months are two complete years, and God delays from the pregnancy what He wills and hastens what He wills.' So Umar was content with my statement."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he used to say: "If a woman gives birth at nine months, twenty-one months of suckling suffice her. If she gives birth at seven months, twenty-three months of suckling suffice her. If she gives birth at six months, then two complete years, because God says: ﴿And its carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him: "This verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq: ﴿until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years, he says: My Lord, enable me﴾, the verse. God answered him, so his parents both embraced Islam, and all his brothers and his children. And concerning him was also revealed ﴿As for he who gives and fears God﴾ [al-Layl: 5], down to the end of the surah."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 46, verse 10–16 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Say: Tell me﴾, i.e., inform me, ﴿if it is from Allah﴾, meaning what is revealed to him of the Qur'an. It was also said that the intended one is Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the meaning is: if he was sent from other than Allah. His saying, "and you have disbelieved in it," is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with qad implied. Likewise His saying, ﴿and a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾. The meaning is: inform me if that is in reality from Allah while you have disbelieved in it, and a witness from the Children of Israel, the knowledgeable ones in what Allah sent down in the Torah, testified to its like, i.e., to the Qur'an, from the meanings present in the Torah that agree with it, such as the affirmation of tawhid, resurrection, rising from the graves, and other things.

This likeness is in terms of the agreement of meanings, even though the wordings differ.

Al-Jurjani said: "mithl" is a connecting particle (ṣilah), and the meaning is: a witness testified concerning it that it is from Allah. Al-Wahidi said the same.

So the witness believed in the Qur'an when it became clear to him that it is the speech of Allah and of the same kind as what He sends down to His messengers. This witness from the Children of Israel is ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, as said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, ʿIkrimah, and others. But this is open to question, for the surah is Meccan by consensus, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam embraced Islam after the Hijrah. So the witness must be a man from the People of the Book who believed in the Qur'an in Mecca and affirmed it. Ibn Jarir chose this view. Later in the discussion there will be what shows that it is ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and that this verse is Medinan, not Meccan.

It is narrated from Masruq that the man intended is Musa (peace be upon him). His saying, "and you were arrogant," is conjoined to "testified": i.e., the witness believed, and you were arrogant about belief. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾: Allah, glory be to Him, deprives them of guidance because of their wronging themselves by disbelief after the clear proof of the obligation of belief has been established. Whoever loses Allah's guidance goes astray.

There has been disagreement about what the answer to the condition is. Al-Zajjaj said it is omitted, its implied meaning being: "Will you then believe?" It was also said that the answer is His saying, ﴿then you believed and were arrogant﴾. It was also said that it is omitted, its implied meaning being: "then you have wronged," as indicated by ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. It was also said that its implied meaning is: "then who is more astray than you," as in His saying: ﴿Tell me, if it is from Allah and you have disbelieved in it, who is more astray?﴾ [Fussilat: 52], and so on.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said its implied meaning is: "Do you feel secure from the punishment of Allah?" It was also said the implied meaning is: "Are you not wrongdoers?"

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another type of their false statements, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said of those who believed﴾, i.e., concerning them. It is possible that this lām is the lām of communication (lām al-tablīgh). ﴿"Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it."﴾ i.e., had what Muhammad brought of the Qur'an and prophethood been good, they would not have preceded us to it, for in their own view they deserved to precede others to every honour. They did not know that Allah, glory be to Him, singles out with His mercy whomever He wills, honours whomever He wills, humbles whomever He wills, and chooses for His religion whomever He wills. ﴿And since they have not been guided by it﴾: i.e., by the Qur'an. It was said: by Muhammad (ﷺ), and it was said: by belief. ﴿They will say, "This is an ancient falsehood."﴾ They went beyond denying the goodness of the Qur'an to claiming that it is an ancient lie, as they said: "Tales of the ancients." The agent of "idh" is an implied verb: i.e., their obstinacy became manifest. The verb "fasayaqulun" cannot govern it, because of the contradiction between the two times, namely the past and the future, and also because of the fa'. It was said that its agent is an implied verb of the same kind as what is mentioned: i.e., "they were not guided by it." And when they were not guided by it, then "they will say."

﴿And before it was the Book of Musa﴾. The majority read the mim of "min" with a kasra, as a preposition, and with its genitive it is a predicate preceding; "the Book of Musa" is a postponed subject. The clause is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial clause, or it is a new independent clause, and the discourse is directed to refute their saying "an ancient falsehood," for the fact that the Book of Musa preceded the Qur'an, and that the two agreed in the foundations of the sharia, shows that it is true and from Allah, and this requires the invalidity of their saying.

It was also read with a fatha on the mim of "man," as a relative pronoun, and with "kitab" in the accusative: i.e., "and We gave to those before him the Book of Musa." This reading is reported from al-Kalbi.

﴿As an imam and a mercy﴾: i.e., one who is followed in religion, and a mercy from Allah for those who believe in it. Both are accusative as circumstantial clauses, as said by al-Zajjaj and others. Al-Akhfash said they are accusative as absolute/detached, and Abu ʿUbayda said: i.e., We made it an imam and a mercy. ﴿And this is a Book confirming﴾: meaning the Qur'an, for it confirms the Book of Musa, which is an imam and a mercy, and other books of Allah. It was also said: it confirms the Prophet (ﷺ). The accusative of ﴿in Arabic tongue﴾ is a preparatory circumstantial clause, its referent being the pronoun in "confirming," which refers to "Book." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be an object of "confirming," but the first is better. It was also said that it is by omission of an annexed noun: i.e., possessor of an Arabic tongue, and this is the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿To warn those who have done wrong﴾. The majority read "liyundhira" with the yā' (third person), its subject being a pronoun referring to the Book: i.e., that the Book warn those who have done wrong. It was also said the pronoun refers to Allah, and it was said to the Messenger, and the first is better.

Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, and al-Bazzi read it with the tā' (second person), its subject being the Prophet (ﷺ). Abu Hatim and Abu ʿUbayd chose this reading. His saying, ﴿and good tidings to the good-doers﴾, is in the place of an accusative, conjoined to the place of "liyundhira." Al-Zajjaj said the better view is that it is in the place of a nominative: i.e., and it is good tidings. It was also said it is in the verbal-noun sense (maṣdar) by an implied verb: i.e., and [it] gives good tidings. His saying "lil-muhsinin" is connected to "bushra."

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast﴾: i.e., they combined tawhid with steadfastness upon the sharia. The explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-Sajdah. ﴿There will be no fear for them﴾: the fa' is extra in the predicate of the relative clause because it has the meaning of a condition. ﴿Nor will they grieve﴾. The meaning: they do not fear that any harm will befall them, nor do they grieve over the loss of something beloved, and that this is continuous and permanent.

﴿Those are the companions of Paradise﴾: i.e., those described with what was mentioned are the companions of Paradise, the abode of believers, while abiding therein forever. It is also said that the two words are the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "They are among the companions of the Garden." ﴿Wa'da al-sidq alladhi kanu yu'adun﴾ ("a true promise which they were promised") is a verbal noun emphasising the content of the preceding sentence, because His saying ﴿Ula'ika alladhina natagabbalu 'anhum﴾ ("Those are they from whom We accept [the best of] what they did") and what follows is in the sense of a promise of acceptance and forgiveness. It may also be a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning: God promised them a true promise, which they were promised through the tongues of the Messengers in this world.

(p-1365) Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim have narrated, and al-Hakim declared it sound, from Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) set out, and I was with him, until we entered the synagogue of the Jews on their day of festival. They disliked our entering upon them. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'O assembly of Jews, show me twelve men from among you who testify that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God; God will remove from every Jew under the canopy of heaven the wrath that is upon him.' They were silent, and none of them answered him. He repeated it to them, and none answered him, three times. He said: 'Have you refused? By God, I am the one who gathers (*al-hashir*), I am the last (*al-'aqib*), and I am the one who follows (*al-muqaffi*). Whether you believe or disbelieve.' Then he turned away, and I was with him, until we were almost leaving. Then a man came from behind him and said: 'Stay as you are, O Muhammad.' So he turned back. That man said: 'What kind of man do you know me to be among you, O assembly of Jews?' They said: 'By God, we know no man among us more knowledgeable in the Book of God, nor more learned, than you, nor than your father, nor than your grandfather.' He said: 'I testify by God that he is the Prophet whom you find written in the Torah and the Gospel.' They said: 'You have lied.' Then they turned against him and said evil things. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'You have lied. Your word will not be accepted from you.' We left, the three of us: the Messenger of God (ﷺ), myself, and Ibn Salam. Then God revealed ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from God and you disbelieve in it...﴾ until His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "I did not hear the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say to anyone walking on the face of the earth that he is among the people of the Garden, except for Abdullah ibn Salam. And concerning him was revealed ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to the like of it﴾."

al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: "Verses of the Book of God were revealed concerning me: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified﴾ was revealed concerning me, and ﴿Say: God is sufficient as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ was revealed concerning me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified﴾ that he said: "It is Abdullah ibn Salam." A similar report has been transmitted from a group of the Followers (*tabi'un*).

In this there is evidence that this verse is Medinan, so the general statement of those who say that the whole of Surat al-Ahqaf is Meccan is to be specified by it.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada, who said: "Some of the polytheists said: 'We are more honourable, and we are, and we are. Had it been good, such-and-such and such-and-such would not have preceded us to it.' So God revealed ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed: Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Awn ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab had a slave-woman who had embraced Islam before him, called Zunayra. Umar used to beat her for her Islam. The disbelieving Quraysh used to say: 'Had it been good, Zunayra would not have preceded us to it.' So God revealed concerning her ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, the verse."

al-Tabarani narrated from Samura ibn Jundub that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "32 Banu Ghifar and Aslam were a trial for many people, who say: 'Had it been good, God would not have made them the first of the people to it.'"

Ibn Asakir narrated through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The statement of Him: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents﴾, the verse, down to His saying: ﴿a true promise which they were promised﴾, was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Nafi' ibn Jubayr that Ibn Abbas informed him, saying: "I am the companion of the woman who was brought to Umar, having given birth after six months. People denied it. I said to Umar: 'Why are you wronging her?' He said: 'How?' I said: 'Recite ﴿And its carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾ and ﴿The mothers suckle their children two complete years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]. How many is the year?' He said: 'A year.' I said: 'How many is the year?' He said: 'Twelve months.' I said: 'Then twenty-four months are two complete years, and God delays from the pregnancy what He wills and hastens what He wills.' So Umar was content with my statement."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he used to say: "If a woman gives birth at nine months, twenty-one months of suckling suffice her. If she gives birth at seven months, twenty-three months of suckling suffice her. If she gives birth at six months, then two complete years, because God says: ﴿And its carrying and weaning is thirty months﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him: "This verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq: ﴿until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years, he says: My Lord, enable me﴾, the verse. God answered him, so his parents both embraced Islam, and all his brothers and his children. And concerning him was also revealed ﴿As for he who gives and fears God﴾ [al-Layl: 5], down to the end of the surah."

When the Exalted mentioned those who give thanks for Allah's blessing upon them and upon their parents, He mentioned the one who said to them a word that indicates impatience with them when they called him to faith. So He said: ﴿And the one who says to his parents, "Uff to you both!"﴾ The relative pronoun (al-ladhi) refers to the category of people who speak that word, and for this reason He referred to him with the plural. "Uff" (uff) is a word that is uttered by a speaker when he is impatient with something that befalls him.

Nafi' and Hafs read "Uffin" (أُفٍّ) with a kasra on the fa' and with tanwin. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a fatha, without tanwin. The rest read it with a kasra, without tanwin. These are dialectal variants. The discussion of this has already been explained in Surat Bani Isra'il (i.e., Surat al-Isra'). The lam in His words "lakuma" (for you both) indicates the object of the expression of annoyance: that is, the expression of annoyance is for you both, as in His words: "Hayta laka" (Yusuf 23), meaning "come, for you."

The majority read "Ata'iddanani" (أتَعِدانِنِي) with two light nuns, and the people of Madina and Makka read its ya' with a fatha, while the rest read it with sukun.

Abu Haywa, al-Mughira and Hisham read with idgham (assimilation) of one of the two nuns into the other, and this reading is narrated from Nafi'.

Al-Hasan, Shayba, Abu Ja'far and 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read the first nun with a fatha, as if they avoided the succession of two kasra-marked identical letters.

The majority read "An ukhraja" (أنْ أُخْرَجَ) with a damma on the hamza and a fatha on the ra', in the passive voice. Al-Hasan, Nasr, Abu al-'Aliya, al-A'mash and Abu Ma'mar read with a fatha on the hamza and a damma on the ra', in the active voice.

The meaning: "Do you promise me that I will be raised after death?" The clause "wa-qad khalati al-qurun min qablí" (And generations have passed away before me) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, while the generations have already passed away before me, they died and none of them was raised. Likewise the clause "wa-huma yastaghithan Allah" (while they both call upon Allah for help) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause: that is, while they both seek Allah's help for him and ask Him to grant him success in faith. "Istaghatha" is transitive by itself and by the preposition bi; it is said: "istaghatha Allah" and "istaghatha bihi."

Al-Razi said: its meaning is "they seek help from Allah against his disbelief," so when the preposition was omitted the verb reached its object directly. It was also said that istighatha means supplication, so there is no need for the preposition bi.

Al-Farra' said: it is said, "Allah answered his supplication and his cry for help" (ajaba Allahu du'a'ahu wa ghiwathahu). His words "Woe to you" (waylaka) are with an implied verb of saying: that is, they say to him, "Woe to you." It is not meant as a curse upon him, but as an urging him to faith. For this reason they said to him: ﴿Believe, for the promise of Allah is true﴾, that is: believe in the resurrection, for the promise of Allah is true, without any failing in it. Thereupon he says, denying what they had said: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the former peoples﴾, that is: what you both say about resurrection is nothing but the tales of the ancients and their falsehoods which they wrote down in books.

The majority read "inna wa'da Allah" (إنَّ وعْدَ اللَّهِ) with a kasra on inna, as a resumption or as a causal clause. 'Umar ibn Fayid and al-A'raj read it with a fatha, taking it as governed by "amin" (believe) with the preposition bi implied: that is, believe that the promise of Allah of resurrection is true.

17. ﴿Those are the ones against whom the word has come into effect﴾, that is: those who utter these statements are the ones against whom the word has come into effect, that is, the punishment has become obligatory for them by the saying of the Exalted to Iblis: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and those among them who follow you, all together﴾ (Sad 85), as His words indicate: ﴿among nations that had passed away before them of jinn and mankind﴾. The clause ﴿Indeed, they were losers﴾ is a justification for what precedes it. This refutes the claim that the cause of the revelation of this verse was 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr, and that he was the one who said to his parents what he said, for he was among the excellent believers and was not among those upon whom the word of punishment took effect. The explanation of the revelation will come at the end of the discussion, if Allah wills.

﴿And for all there are degrees according to what they did﴾, that is: for each of the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, among jinn and mankind, there are ranks with Allah on the Day of Resurrection according to their deeds.

Ibn Zayd said: the degrees of the people of the Fire in this verse go downward, and the degrees of the people of Paradise go upward. ﴿And that He may fully repay them for their deeds﴾, that is: the recompense for their deeds.

The majority read "li-nuwaffiyahum" (لِنُوَفِّيَهم) with nun. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with the yā' (third person).

Abu 'Ubayd preferred the first reading, and Abu Hatim preferred the second.

﴿And they will not be wronged﴾, that is: the evildoer will not be increased in punishment, nor will the doer of good be diminished in reward; rather each group will be paid in full what it deserves of good and evil. The clause is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause, or it is a resumed clause confirming what precedes it.

﴿And [mention] the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire﴾. The adverbial phrase is connected to an implied verb: that is, mention to them, O Muhammad, the day when the covering is removed, so they see the Fire and draw near to it. It was also said that the meaning of "yu'radun" is "they will be tormented," from the expression "'aradahu 'ala al-sayf" (he exposed him to the sword). It was also said that there is inversion (qalb) in the speech.

The meaning: the Fire will be exposed to them. ﴿"You squandered your good things in your worldly life"﴾, that is: it will be said to them this. It was said that this implied verb is what governs the adverbial phrase, but the first is preferable. The majority read "adhhabtum" (أذْهَبْتُمْ) with a single hamza. Al-Hasan, Nasr, Abu al-'Aliya, Ya'qub and Ibn Kathir read it with two light hamzas. The meaning of the interrogative is reproach and rebuke.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs rebuke by means of the interrogative and by other means, so the rebuke is present in both readings.

Al-Kalbi said: what is meant by "the good things" is pleasures and the livelihoods they were in. ﴿And you enjoyed them﴾, that is, the good things. The meaning is that they followed the desires and pleasures that were in disobedience to Allah the Exalted, and did not care about sin, denying what the messengers had brought of the promise of reckoning, punishment and reward. ﴿So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾, that is: the punishment in which there is disgrace for you and shame upon you.

Mujahid and Qatada said: "al-Hun" is "al-Hawan" in the dialect of Quraysh.

﴿Because you were arrogant in the earth without right﴾, that is: because of your arrogance against worshipping Allah and believing in Him and affirming His oneness. ﴿And because you used to defy [Allah]﴾, that is: you went out of obedience to Allah and did His disobedience. Thus He made the cause of their punishment two things: arrogance against following the truth, and acting in disobedience to Allah the Exalted. This is the condition of the disbelievers, for they have combined both of them.

Al-Bukhari has narrated from Yusuf ibn Mahak who said: Marwan was over the Hijaz, appointed by Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan. He gave a sermon and began to mention Yazid ibn Mu'awiya, so that allegiance would be pledged to him after his father. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr said something, so Marwan said, "Seize him!" He entered the house of 'A'isha, and they could not reach him. Marwan said: "This was revealed concerning him: ﴿And the one who says to his parents, 'Uff to you both!'﴾." 'A'isha said: "Allah did not reveal anything concerning us of the Qur'an except that Allah revealed my innocence."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh have narrated from Muhammad ibn Ziyad who said: When Mu'awiya pledged allegiance for his son, Marwan said: "It is the sunna of Abu Bakr and 'Umar." 'Abd al-Rahman said: "It is the sunna of Heraclius and Caesar." Marwan said: "This is the one about whom Allah said: ﴿And the one who says to his parents, 'Uff to you both!'﴾," the verse. This reached 'A'isha, and she said: "Marwan lied, by Allah, it is not about him. If I wished to name the one about whom it was revealed, I would name him. But the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed the father of Marwan, while Marwan was in his loins, so Marwan is one whom Allah has cursed."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse that he said: "This is a son of Abu Bakr."

Abu Hatim narrated similarly from al-Suddi, but this is not authentic, as we have previously mentioned.
