Al-Razi said: its meaning is "they seek help from Allah against his disbelief," so when the preposition was omitted the verb reached its object directly. It was also said that istighatha means supplication, so there is no need for the preposition bi.

Al-Farra' said: it is said, "Allah answered his supplication and his cry for help" (ajaba Allahu du'a'ahu wa ghiwathahu). His words "Woe to you" (waylaka) are with an implied verb of saying: that is, they say to him, "Woe to you." It is not meant as a curse upon him, but as an urging him to faith. For this reason they said to him: ﴿Believe, for the promise of Allah is true﴾, that is: believe in the resurrection, for the promise of Allah is true, without any failing in it. Thereupon he says, denying what they had said: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the former peoples﴾, that is: what you both say about resurrection is nothing but the tales of the ancients and their falsehoods which they wrote down in books.

The majority read "inna wa'da Allah" (إنَّ وعْدَ اللَّهِ) with a kasra on inna, as a resumption or as a causal clause. 'Umar ibn Fayid and al-A'raj read it with a fatha, taking it as governed by "amin" (believe) with the preposition bi implied: that is, believe that the promise of Allah of resurrection is true.

17. ﴿Those are the ones against whom the word has come into effect﴾, that is: those who utter these statements are the ones against whom the word has come into effect, that is, the punishment has become obligatory for them by the saying of the Exalted to Iblis: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and those among them who follow you, all together﴾ (Sad 85), as His words indicate: ﴿among nations that had passed away before them of jinn and mankind﴾. The clause ﴿Indeed, they were losers﴾ is a justification for what precedes it. This refutes the claim that the cause of the revelation of this verse was 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr, and that he was the one who said to his parents what he said, for he was among the excellent believers and was not among those upon whom the word of punishment took effect. The explanation of the revelation will come at the end of the discussion, if Allah wills.

﴿And for all there are degrees according to what they did﴾, that is: for each of the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, among jinn and mankind, there are ranks with Allah on the Day of Resurrection according to their deeds.

Ibn Zayd said: the degrees of the people of the Fire in this verse go downward, and the degrees of the people of Paradise go upward. ﴿And that He may fully repay them for their deeds﴾, that is: the recompense for their deeds.

The majority read "li-nuwaffiyahum" (لِنُوَفِّيَهم) with nun. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with the yā' (third person).

Abu 'Ubayd preferred the first reading, and Abu Hatim preferred the second.

﴿And they will not be wronged﴾, that is: the evildoer will not be increased in punishment, nor will the doer of good be diminished in reward; rather each group will be paid in full what it deserves of good and evil. The clause is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause, or it is a resumed clause confirming what precedes it.

﴿And [mention] the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire﴾. The adverbial phrase is connected to an implied verb: that is, mention to them, O Muhammad, the day when the covering is removed, so they see the Fire and draw near to it. It was also said that the meaning of "yu'radun" is "they will be tormented," from the expression "'aradahu 'ala al-sayf" (he exposed him to the sword). It was also said that there is inversion (qalb) in the speech.

The meaning: the Fire will be exposed to them. ﴿"You squandered your good things in your worldly life"﴾, that is: it will be said to them this. It was said that this implied verb is what governs the adverbial phrase, but the first is preferable. The majority read "adhhabtum" (أذْهَبْتُمْ) with a single hamza. Al-Hasan, Nasr, Abu al-'Aliya, Ya'qub and Ibn Kathir read it with two light hamzas. The meaning of the interrogative is reproach and rebuke.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the Arabs rebuke by means of the interrogative and by other means, so the rebuke is present in both readings.

Al-Kalbi said: what is meant by "the good things" is pleasures and the livelihoods they were in. ﴿And you enjoyed them﴾, that is, the good things. The meaning is that they followed the desires and pleasures that were in disobedience to Allah the Exalted, and did not care about sin, denying what the messengers had brought of the promise of reckoning, punishment and reward. ﴿So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾, that is: the punishment in which there is disgrace for you and shame upon you.

Mujahid and Qatada said: "al-Hun" is "al-Hawan" in the dialect of Quraysh.

﴿Because you were arrogant in the earth without right﴾, that is: because of your arrogance against worshipping Allah and believing in Him and affirming His oneness. ﴿And because you used to defy [Allah]﴾, that is: you went out of obedience to Allah and did His disobedience. Thus He made the cause of their punishment two things: arrogance against following the truth, and acting in disobedience to Allah the Exalted. This is the condition of the disbelievers, for they have combined both of them.

Al-Bukhari has narrated from Yusuf ibn Mahak who said: Marwan was over the Hijaz, appointed by Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan. He gave a sermon and began to mention Yazid ibn Mu'awiya, so that allegiance would be pledged to him after his father. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr said something, so Marwan said, "Seize him!" He entered the house of 'A'isha, and they could not reach him. Marwan said: "This was revealed concerning him: ﴿And the one who says to his parents, 'Uff to you both!'﴾." 'A'isha said: "Allah did not reveal anything concerning us of the Qur'an except that Allah revealed my innocence."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh have narrated from Muhammad ibn Ziyad who said: When Mu'awiya pledged allegiance for his son, Marwan said: "It is the sunna of Abu Bakr and 'Umar." 'Abd al-Rahman said: "It is the sunna of Heraclius and Caesar." Marwan said: "This is the one about whom Allah said: ﴿And the one who says to his parents, 'Uff to you both!'﴾," the verse. This reached 'A'isha, and she said: "Marwan lied, by Allah, it is not about him. If I wished to name the one about whom it was revealed, I would name him. Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse that he said: "This is a son of Abu Bakr."

Abu Hatim narrated similarly from al-Suddi, but this is not authentic, as we have previously mentioned.

When the Exalted mentioned those who give thanks for Allah's blessing upon them and upon their parents, He mentioned the one who said to them a word that indicates impatience with them when they called him to faith. So He said: ﴿And the one who says to his parents, "Uff to you both!"﴾ The relative pronoun (al-ladhi) refers to the category of people who speak that word, and for this reason He referred to him with the plural. "Uff" (uff) is a word that is uttered by a speaker when he is impatient with something that befalls him.

Nafi' and Hafs read "Uffin" (أُفٍّ) with a kasra on the fa' and with tanwin. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a fatha, without tanwin. The rest read it with a kasra, without tanwin. These are dialectal variants. The discussion of this has already been explained in Surat Bani Isra'il (i.e., Surat al-Isra'). The lam in His words "lakuma" (for you both) indicates the object of the expression of annoyance: that is, the expression of annoyance is for you both, as in His words: "Hayta laka" (Yusuf 23), meaning "come, for you."

The majority read "Ata'iddanani" (أتَعِدانِنِي) with two light nuns, and the people of Madina and Makka read its ya' with a fatha, while the rest read it with sukun.

Abu Haywa, al-Mughira and Hisham read with idgham (assimilation) of one of the two nuns into the other, and this reading is narrated from Nafi'.

Al-Hasan, Shayba, Abu Ja'far and 'Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, read the first nun with a fatha, as if they avoided the succession of two kasra-marked identical letters.

The majority read "An ukhraja" (أنْ أُخْرَجَ) with a damma on the hamza and a fatha on the ra', in the passive voice. Al-Hasan, Nasr, Abu al-'Aliya, al-A'mash and Abu Ma'mar read with a fatha on the hamza and a damma on the ra', in the active voice.

The meaning: "Do you promise me that I will be raised after death?" The clause "wa-qad khalati al-qurun min qablí" (And generations have passed away before me) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, while the generations have already passed away before me, they died and none of them was raised. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 46, verses 21–28:

(p-1367) His saying: ﴿And mention the brother of ʿĀd﴾ means: and mention, O Muhammad, to your people the brother of ʿĀd, who was Hūd son of ʿAbd Allāh son of Rabāḥ. He was their brother in lineage, not in religion. His saying: ﴿when he warned his people﴾ is a badal ishtimāl (an inclusive apposition) from it, meaning: at the time of his warning them in al-Aḥqāf, which are the dwellings of ʿĀd. Aḥqāf is the plural of ḥiqf, which is a great, elongated, curved sand dune, as said by al-Khalīl and others. They had overpowered the people of the earth by their strength. The meaning is that Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to recount to his people their story so that they would take heed and fear. It was also said that he was commanded to reflect within himself upon their story with Hūd, so that he might follow it as an example and so that the denial of his people would be easier for him to bear.

ʿAṭāʾ said: al-Aḥqāf are the sand dunes of the land of al-Shiḥr.

Muqātil said: they are in Yemen, in Ḥaḍramawt. Ibn Zayd said: they are extended sands spread out, in the form of mountains, but they did not reach being mountains. ﴿And warners had passed away before him and after him﴾ means: messengers had passed away before him and would come after him. So said al-Farrāʾ and others.

In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd: ( ﴿from before him and from behind him﴾ ), and the clause is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) in the accusative. It is permissible that it be a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍiyyah) between the warning of Hūd and his saying to his people: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾. The first is preferable.

The meaning: he informed them that the messengers who were sent before him and those who would be sent after him are all warners like his warning. Then he returned to Hūd's speech to his people, and so he said, relating from him: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾. It was also said that making that clause parenthetical is more fitting to the context and more in accord with the meaning.

﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away from our gods?"﴾ means: to divert us from worshipping them. It was also said: to remove us, and it was said: to prevent us. The meanings are close. From it is the saying of ʿUrwah ibn Udhaynah:

If you are turned away from good conduct,
then among others who have been turned away (uftika) you are.

He says: if you are not granted success in doing good, you are among a people who have been diverted from that. ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾ of the great punishment ﴿if you are of the truthful﴾ in your promise to us regarding it.

﴿He said: "The knowledge is only with Allah"﴾ meaning: the knowledge of the time of its coming is only with Allah, not with me. ﴿And I convey to you what I have been sent with﴾ from your Lord, of warning and admonition. As for knowledge of the time of the coming of the punishment, He has not revealed it to me. ﴿But I see you to be a people who are ignorant﴾ in that you remain persistent in your disbelief and have not been guided by what I brought you, rather you have proposed to me what is not among the duties of messengers.

23. ﴿And when they saw it as a cloud approaching their valleys﴾ The pronoun refers to "mā" in His saying: "with what you threaten us."

Al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjāj said: the pronoun in "raʾawhu" refers to something not mentioned, and His saying "ʿāriḍan" clarifies it. So the pronoun refers to the cloud: that is, when they saw the cloud as ʿāriḍan (approaching). "ʿāriḍan" is in the accusative as a repetition, meaning an explanation. The cloud was called ʿāriḍ because it appears across the breadth of the sky.

Al-Jawharī said: al-ʿāriḍ is the cloud that spreads across the horizon, and from it is His saying: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾. The accusative of "ʿāriḍan" is either as a ḥāl or as a tamyīz. ﴿Approaching their valleys﴾ means: heading toward their valleys.

The exegetes said: ʿĀd had been held back from rain for days, so Allah drove to them a black cloud, and it emerged over them from a valley of theirs called al-Maʿtab. When they saw it approaching their valleys, they rejoiced, and ﴿they said, "This is a cloud bringing us rain."﴾ meaning: a cloud containing rain. His saying "approaching their valleys" is an adjective of "ʿāriḍ," because its idafah is verbal, not semantic, so it is valid to describe an indefinite noun by it. Likewise "bringing us rain." When they said that, Hūd answered them, saying: ﴿Rather, it is what you were hasty about﴾, meaning the punishment, since they said: ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾. His saying "rīḥ" (wind) is either a badal from "mā," or the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause ﴿in it is a painful punishment﴾ is an adjective of "rīḥ." The wind by which they were punished arose from that very cloud they had seen.

﴿Destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾ This clause is a second adjective of "rīḥ": that is, it destroys everything it passed over, of the lives and property of ʿĀd. Tadmīr means destruction, as does dammār. It was read as "yudmuru" with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, sukūn on the dāl, ḍammah on the mīm, and raf` of "kull" as the subject, from damara, damāran. The meaning of "by the command of its Lord" is that this occurred by His decree and destiny. ﴿So they became such that nothing was seen except their dwellings﴾, meaning that you, O Muhammad, or anyone fit for seeing, would not see anything except their dwellings after their selves and property had perished.

The majority read "lā tarā" with the second-person form (tāʾ), and an accusative "masākinahum."

Ḥamzah and ʿĀṣim read it with the yāʾ, damma, in the passive voice, and a nominative "masākinuhum."

Sībawayh said: its meaning is that their persons are not seen, only their dwellings. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the second reading.

Al-Kisāʾī and al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is that nothing is seen except their dwellings. It is construed according to meaning, as when you say: "No one stood except Hind," meaning: no one stood except Hind. There is an omission in the speech, the supposed sense being: the wind came upon them and destroyed them, so they became such that nothing was seen except their dwellings. ﴿Thus do We recompense the criminal people﴾, meaning: We recompense these people with a like recompense. The account of this story has already been explained in Surah al-Aʿrāf.

﴿And We had certainly established them in that in which We have not established you﴾ Al-Mubarrad said: "mā" in His saying "fīmā" is in the position of "alladhī" (which), and "in" is in the position of "mā," i.e., the negating particle. Its estimate: "And We had certainly established them in that which We did not establish you in, of wealth, length of life, and strength of bodies." It was said: "in" is superfluous, and its estimate: "And We had certainly established them in that in which We established you," and al-Qutaybī said so, and a similar saying is the poet's:

"Indeed, it was not cowardice that made them [their women] incline, but our fates and the state of others."

The first is preferable, because it is more forceful in rebuking the disbelievers of Quraysh and their like. ﴿And We made for them hearing and sight and hearts﴾, meaning: they turned away from accepting proof and reflection, despite what Allah had given them of the senses by which evidence is perceived. For this reason He said: ﴿But their hearing did not avail them, nor their sight, nor their hearts, in anything﴾, meaning: what Allah had given them of these did not benefit them, since they did not use it to reach monotheism and the truth of the promise and threat. We have already mentioned, in discussing the form of singular "hearing" and plural "sight," what suffices without repetition. The "min" in "min shayʾ" is superfluous, the estimate being: nothing of availing availed them, nor did it benefit them in any way of benefit. (p-1368) ﴿Since they used to deny the signs of Allah﴾: the adverbial clause is connected to "aghnā," and it carries the sense of causation, meaning: because they used to deny. ﴿And there encompassed them what they used to mock﴾, meaning: the punishment they were hastening, by way of mockery, encompassed them, since they said: ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾.

﴿And We had certainly destroyed what is around you of the towns﴾ The address is to the people of Makkah, and what is around them of towns refers to the towns of Thamūd, the towns of Lot, and the like, which bordered the land of the Ḥijāz, and their reports were widely known to them. ﴿And We diversified the signs that they might return﴾, meaning: We explained the proofs and varied them so that they would return from their disbelief, but they did not return.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned that no helper would defend them from the punishment of Allah, saying: ﴿So why did not those they had taken as gods besides Allah, as offerings, support them?﴾ meaning: why did not their gods, through which they sought nearness to Allah according to their claim, support them, so as to intercede for them, since they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾, and prevent them from the destruction that befell them.

Al-Kisāʾī said: qurbān is everything by which one draws near to Allah, of obedience or sacrifice. Its plural is qarābīn, like rahbān and rahābīn. One of the two objects of "ittakhadhū" is a pronoun referring to the relative, and the second is "ālihatan." "Qurbānan" is a ḥāl. It is not valid for "qurbānan" to be a second object with "ālihatan" as its badal, due to the corruption of meaning. It was said that this is valid and does not corrupt the meaning. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Abū al-Baqāʾ, and Abū Ḥayyān preferred this, and denied that there is corruption of meaning on this view.

﴿Rather, they strayed from them﴾, meaning: they were absent from their support and did not come forward when they were needed. It was also said: rather they perished. It was also said: the pronoun in "ḍallū" refers to the disbelievers, meaning: they abandoned the idols and disowned them. The first is preferable. The indication in His saying "and that" refers to the straying of their gods.

The meaning: that straying and loss was the effect of their falsehood, which is their taking them as gods and their claim that they bring them near to Allah.

The majority read "ifkuhum" with a kasrah on the hamzah and sukūn on the fāʾ, the verbal noun of afika, yafику, ifkan, meaning: their lie.

Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Mujāhid read it with fatḥah on the hamzah, the fāʾ, and the kāf, as a verb: that is, that saying diverted them from monotheism.

ʿIkrimah read it with fatḥah on the hamzah and tashdīd on the fāʾ: that is, he made them turners-away (āfikīn).

Abū Ḥātim said: it means he turned them from the bounty they had been upon. There is an omission in the speech, the supposed sense being: the wind came upon them and destroyed them, so they became such that nothing was seen except their dwellings. ﴿Thus do We recompense the criminal people﴾, meaning: We recompense these people with a like recompense. The account of this story has already been explained in Surah al-Aʿrāf.

﴿And We had certainly established them in that in which We have not established you﴾ Al-Mubarrad said: "mā" in His saying "fīmā" is in the position of "alladhī" (which), and "in" is in the position of "mā," i.e., the negating particle. Its estimate: "And We had certainly established them in that which We did not establish you in, of wealth, length of life, and strength of bodies." It was said: "in" is superfluous, and its estimate: "And We had certainly established them in that in which We established you," and al-Qutaybī said so, and a similar saying is the poet's:

"Indeed, it was not cowardice that made them [their women] incline, but our fates and the state of others."

The first is preferable, because it is more forceful in rebuking the disbelievers of Quraysh and their like. ﴿And We made for them hearing and sight and hearts﴾, meaning: they turned away from accepting proof and reflection, despite what Allah had given them of the senses by which evidence is perceived. But when they first recognized that it was a punishment, they saw that men and livestock of theirs were flying between the sky and the earth like feathers. They entered their houses and locked their doors, but the wind came and opened their doors and sent the sand upon them, so they were under the sand seven nights and eight days, continuously, with groaning. Then Allah commanded the wind, and it uncovered the sand from them and cast them into the sea. This is His saying: ﴿So they became such that nothing was seen except their dwellings.﴾

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: Allah sent upon ʿĀd no wind except the measure of this ring of mine.

Muqātil said: they are in Yemen, in Ḥaḍramawt. The first is preferable.

The meaning: he informed them that the messengers who were sent before him and those who would be sent after him are all warners like his warning. It was also said that making that clause parenthetical is more fitting to the context and more in accord with the meaning.

﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away from our gods?"﴾ means: to divert us from worshipping them. It was also said: to remove us, and it was said: to prevent us. The meanings are close. From it is the saying of ʿUrwah ibn Udhaynah:

If you are turned away from good conduct,
then among others who have been turned away (uftika) you are.

He says: if you are not granted success in doing good, you are among a people who have been diverted from that. ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾ of the great punishment ﴿if you are of the truthful﴾ in your promise to us regarding it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 46, verses 29–35 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glorified is He, made clear that among mankind there are those who believed and among them those who disbelieved, He also made clear that the same is true of the jinn. So He said: ﴿And [mention] when We directed to you a company of the jinn, listening to the Qur'an.﴾ The verb governing the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is implied: that is, "and remember when We directed," i.e., We turned toward you a company of the jinn and sent them to you. His words ﴿listening to the Qur'an﴾ are in the accusative position as a second attribute (sifah) of "nafaran" (a company), or as a circumstantial state (hal), because the indefinite noun has been specified by the first attribute. (p-1369) ﴿When they attended it﴾: that is, they attended the Qur'an at its recitation. It has also been said they attended the Prophet (ﷺ), and in that case there is an iltifat (shift) in the speech from address (khitab) to third person (ghaybah). The first is more preferable. ﴿They said, "Be silent."﴾ That is, some of them said to others, "Be silent," urging one another to this so that they might listen. ﴿So when it was concluded﴾: Al-Jumhur read (quddiya) in the passive voice, meaning it was finished, i.e., its recitation was completed.

Habib ibn Ubayd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Lahiq ibn Humayd, and Abu Mijlaz read it in the active voice, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ) finished its recitation. The first reading supports that the pronoun in "hadarūhu" refers to the Qur'an, while the second reading supports that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿They turned back to their people as warners﴾: that is, they departed, intending toward those behind them among their people, warning them against opposing the Qur'an and cautioning them. The accusative of "mundhirin" is a circumstantial state (hal muqaddarah), meaning they intended to warn. This indicates that they believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), and the explanation of that will come at the end of the discussion.

﴿They said, "O our people, indeed we have heard a Book revealed after Moses"﴾: they mean the Qur'an. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning is: so they reached their people and said, "O our people."

ʿAtaʾ said: They were Jews and then they embraced Islam. ﴿Confirming what came before it﴾: that is, the previously revealed books. ﴿It guides to the truth﴾: that is, to the true religion. ﴿And to a straight path﴾: that is, to the upright path of Allah.

Muqatil said: Allah did not send a prophet to the jinn and mankind before Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in him﴾: they mean Muhammad (ﷺ), or the Qur'an. ﴿He will forgive you of your sins﴾: that is, some of them, namely what is other than the rights of people. It has been said that "min" here is for the beginning of the extent (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). The meaning is: forgiveness of sins begins and then ends with forgiveness of leaving what is preferable. It has also been said that it is superfluous (za'idah). ﴿And protect you from a painful punishment﴾: which is the punishment of the Fire. In this verse is evidence that the ruling for the jinn is the ruling for mankind regarding reward and punishment and being bound by commands and prohibitions.

Al-Hasan said: The believing jinn have no reward other than their salvation from the Fire, and Abu Hanifah said likewise.

The first view is preferable, and Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ibn Abi Layla held it.

According to the first view, those who hold it say that after their salvation from the Fire, it will be said to them: "Be dust," as is said to the beasts. The second is more likely.

Allah, glorified is He, has said in addressing the jinn and mankind: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens. So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 46–47]. So Allah, glorified is He, bestowed favor upon both weighty groups by making the reward of their good-doers the Garden. This restriction here to mention of their protection from a painful punishment does not contradict that. Among what supports this is that Allah, glorified is He, has repaid their disbelievers with the Fire, which is a station of justice; so how would He not repay their good-doers with the Garden, which is a station of bounty? Also among what supports this is what the noble Qur'an says in more than one place: the reward of believers is the Garden, the reward of those who do righteous deeds is the Garden, the reward of whoever says "There is no god but Allah" is the Garden, and other things that are numerous in the Book and the Sunnah.

The scholars have differed over whether Allah sent messengers to the jinn from among themselves or not. The apparent meaning of the Qur'anic verses is that the messengers were from mankind only, as in His saying: ﴿And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed, from the people of the towns﴾ [Yusuf: 109]. And He said: ﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]. And He, glorified is He, said about Abraham the Friend: ﴿And We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book﴾, so every prophet Allah sent after Abraham is of his descendants. ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah will not escape [Him] on earth﴾: that is, he cannot outrun Allah, nor escape Him, nor is he able to flee from Him; for even if he flees every way, he is on the earth and has no path to exit from it. In this is a severe warning. ﴿And he will not have any protectors besides Him﴾: that is, helpers who will prevent him from the punishment of Allah. After explaining the impossibility of his being saved by himself, Allah, glorified is He, made clear the impossibility of his being saved through another. The indication by His words "those" (ulaʾika) refers to "whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah," and He informed that they are ﴿in manifest error﴾: that is, clear and evident.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned evidence for resurrection, saying: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and was not exhausted by their creation...﴾ The seeing here is the heart-seeing meaning knowledge, and the interrogative hamzah is for denial, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied element: that is, did they not reflect and did they not know that He who created these great bodies, the heavens and the earth, originally? ﴿And He was not incapable of their creation﴾: that is, He was not unable to do that, nor was He weakened by it. It is said "ʿayya bi-l-amr" and "ʿayiya," when one is not guided to its way. From this is the poet's saying:

Al-Jumhur read (wa-lam yaʿya) with a sukun on the ʿayn and a fatha on the yāʾ, as the present tense of ʿayiya. Al-Hasan read with a kasra on the ʿayn and sukun on the yāʾ. ﴿Is not able to give life to the dead?﴾: Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Akhfash said the bāʾ is superfluous for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as witness﴾. In this command to them to taste the punishment is severe reproach and great mockery.

It has also been said that all the messengers are of determination, and it has been said they are twelve prophets sent to the Children of Israel.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 46, verses 29–35 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Masruq, who said: I asked Ibn Mas'ud, "Who informed the Prophet (ﷺ) about the jinn on the night they listened to the Qur'an?" He said: "A tree informed him of them."

He said: "None of us accompanied him. But we missed him one night and said, 'He has been seized, or carried off. What has happened to him?' So we spent the worst night any people ever spent. When it was the dawn, behold, he came from the direction of Hira. We told him, and he said: 'The messenger of the jinn came to me, so I went to them and recited the Qur'an to them.' Then he set off, and he showed us their traces and the traces of their fires."

Something similar has been related through several chains.

This indicates that they believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), and the explanation of that will come at the end of the discussion.

Muqatil said: Allah did not send a prophet to the jinn and mankind before Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daylami related from ʿA'isha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fasted continuously, then he broke his fast, then he fasted continuously again, then he broke it, then he fasted continuously again," and he said: "O ʿA'isha, indeed this world is not fitting for Muhammad or the family of Muhammad. O ʿA'isha, indeed Allah was not pleased with the ulu al-'azm among the messengers except through patience in what is disliked and patience in refraining from what is loved. Then He was not pleased with me except that He would burden me with what He burdened them with. So He said: ﴿So be patient as the ulu al-'azm among the messengers were patient﴾. By Allah, I shall indeed be patient as they were patient, to the utmost of my ability. And there is no power except by Allah."

So He said: ﴿And [mention] when We directed to you a company of the jinn, listening to the Qur'an.﴾ The verb governing the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is implied: that is, "and remember when We directed," i.e., We turned toward you a company of the jinn and sent them to you. (p-1369) ﴿When they attended it﴾: that is, they attended the Qur'an at its recitation. This indicates that they believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), and the explanation of that will come at the end of the discussion.

﴿They said, "O our people, indeed we have heard a Book revealed after Moses"﴾: they mean the Qur'an. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning is: so they reached their people and said, "O our people."

It has also been said that it is superfluous (za'idah). ﴿And protect you from a painful punishment﴾: which is the punishment of the Fire. Al-Hasan said: The believing jinn have no reward other than their salvation from the Fire, and Abu Hanifah said likewise.

The first view is preferable, and Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ibn Abi Layla held it.

According to the first view, those who hold it say that after their salvation from the Fire, it will be said to them: "Be dust," as is said to the beasts. The second is more likely.

And He said: ﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]. And He, glorified is He, said about Abraham the Friend: ﴿And We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book﴾, so every prophet Allah sent after Abraham is of his descendants. The indication by His words "those" (ulaʾika) refers to "whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah," and He informed that they are ﴿in manifest error﴾: that is, clear and evident.

They were baffled by their affair as the dove was baffled by its egg.

Al-Hasan read with a kasra on the ʿayn and sukun on the yāʾ. ﴿Is not able to give life to the dead?﴾: Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Akhfash said the bāʾ is superfluous for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as witness﴾. In this command to them to taste the punishment is severe reproach and great mockery.

When Allah, glorified is He, established the proofs for prophethood, monotheism, and the return, He commanded His Messenger to be patient, saying: ﴿So be patient as the messengers of determination were patient﴾. The "fa" is the answer to an implied condition: that is, when you have known this, and the proofs have been established for it, and it has not been effective upon the disbelievers, then be patient as the people of determination were patient, i.e., the possessors of steadfastness and resolve, for you are among them.

Mujahid said: The messengers of determination are five: Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad (ﷺ), and they are the possessors of the sacred laws (ashab al-shara'i').

Abu al-ʿAliyah said: They are Noah, Hud, and Abraham, and Allah commanded His Messenger that he be the fourth of them.

Al-Suddi said: They are six: Abraham, Moses, David, Solomon, Jesus, and Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said: Noah, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Lot, and Moses.

Ibn Jurayj said: Among them are Ishmael, Jacob, and Job, and Jonah is not among them.

Al-Sha'bi and al-Kalbi said: They are those who were commanded to fight, who manifested open confrontation and fought the disbelievers. It has also been said they are the noble messengers mentioned in Surat al-An'am, and they are eighteen: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Noah, David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, Zechariah, John, Jesus, Elias, Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl chose this, based on His saying after mentioning them: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. It has also been said that all the messengers are of determination, and it has been said they are twelve prophets sent to the Children of Israel.

Al-Hasan said: They are four: Abraham, Moses, David, and Jesus.

﴿And do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them﴾: that is, do not seek to hasten the punishment for the disbelievers, O Muhammad.

When Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to be patient and forbade him from seeking to hasten punishment for his people, hoping they would believe, He said: ﴿As if, the Day they see what they were promised [of punishment], they had not remained [in the world] except an hour of a day﴾: that is, as if on the Day they witness it in the Hereafter, they had not remained in the world except the measure of an hour of the hours of the days, because of the great terror and the lasting affliction they witness.

Al-Jumhur read (balagh) with a raf', as the predicate of an implied subject: that is, this which I have admonished them with is a message, or that hour is a message, or this Qur'an is a message, or it is a subject whose predicate is "for them," following His saying "do not hasten": that is, for them is a message. Al-Hasan, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, and Zayd ibn ʿAli read (balaghan) with a fatha, as a verbal noun: that is, convey a conveyance. Abu Mijlaz read (balligh) in the imperative form. It has also been read (ballagha) in the past form. ﴿So will any be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾ Al-Jumhur read (fa-hal yuhlaku) in the passive voice. Ibn Muhaysin read it in the active voice, and the meaning is that none will be destroyed by the punishment of Allah except the people who depart from obedience and fall into the sins of Allah.

Qatadah said: None will perish before Allah except a polytheist who perishes.

It has been said: this verse is the strongest verse in hope.

Al-Zajjaj said: Its interpretation is: none will perish, together with the mercy and grace of Allah, except the defiantly disobedient people.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Mani', al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, both report from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: They descended, meaning the jinn, upon the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was reciting the Qur'an in the valley of Nakhlah. When they heard it, they said, "Be silent," and they said, "Shh." They were nine, one of whom was Zawba'ah. So Allah revealed: ﴿And [mention] when We directed to you a company of the jinn...﴾ up to His words "in manifest error."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh report from al-Zubayr: ﴿And [mention] when We directed to you a company of the jinn, listening to the Qur'an﴾, he said: at Nakhlah, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was praying the late night prayer ʿIshaʾ. ﴿They almost became, against him, a compacted mass﴾ [al-Jinn: 19].

Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh report ﴿And [mention] when We directed to you a company of the jinn﴾ the verse. He said: They were nine men from the people of Nasibin, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made them messengers to their people.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nu'aym also report something similar, saying: The jinn were turned toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) twice, and they were the nobles of the jinn at Nasibin.

Something similar has been related through several chains.

It has also been said that all the messengers are of determination, and it has been said they are twelve prophets sent to the Children of Israel.

Ibn Muhaysin read it in the active voice, and the meaning is that none will be destroyed by the punishment of Allah except the people who depart from obedience and fall into the sins of Allah.

Qatadah said: None will perish before Allah except a polytheist who perishes.

Al-Zajjaj said: Its interpretation is: none will perish, together with the mercy and grace of Allah, except the defiantly disobedient people.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Masruq, who said: I asked Ibn Mas'ud, "Who informed the Prophet (ﷺ) about the jinn on the night they listened to the Qur'an?" He said: "A tree informed him of them."

Ibn Mardawayh also related from him, who said: they are those who were commanded to fight until they passed away upon that: Nuh, Hud, Salih, Musa, Dawud and Sulayman.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daylami related from ʿA'isha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fasted continuously, then he broke his fast, then he fasted continuously again, then he broke it, then he fasted continuously again," and he said: "O ʿA'isha, indeed this world is not fitting for Muhammad or the family of Muhammad. Many hadiths also report that the jinn later came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) several times and took the laws (shara'i') from him.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: concerning ﴿the ulu al-'azm (possessors of resolve) among the messengers﴾: they are the Prophet (ﷺ), Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa.

Ibn Mardawayh also related from him, who said: they are those who were commanded to fight until they passed away upon that: Nuh, Hud, Salih, Musa, Dawud and Sulayman.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: "It has reached me that the ulu al-'azm among the messengers were three hundred and thirteen."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daylami related from ʿA'isha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fasted continuously, then he broke his fast, then he fasted continuously again, then he broke it, then he fasted continuously again," and he said: "O ʿA'isha, indeed this world is not fitting for Muhammad or the family of Muhammad. O ʿA'isha, indeed Allah was not pleased with the ulu al-'azm among the messengers except through patience in what is disliked and patience in refraining from what is loved. Then He was not pleased with me except that He would burden me with what He burdened them with. So He said: ﴿So be patient as the ulu al-'azm among the messengers were patient﴾. By Allah, I shall indeed be patient as they were patient, to the utmost of my ability. And there is no power except by Allah."
